name: Nigeria
summary_text: Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks. A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

sources.title: Abuja Area Mama, Nigerian transgender TikToker, found dead
sources.claim_summary: BBC (Aug 2024): Nigerian trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama' found dead - her beaten body was found along an Abuja highway hours after posting about going to see her boyfriend; she had previously expressed fears for her life. Police described her as 'a man fully dressed in female clothing'; same-sex relationships are criminalised in Nigeria and perceived-gay TikTokers face homophobic abuse online.

sources.title: Threats, Raids and Potlucks — The Dial
sources.claim_summary: The Dial (Feb 2025): 'Threats, Raids and Potlucks' - reporting on what it's like to be queer in Nigeria, centred on Abuja Area Mama's killing; six months later no suspects charged; the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation; transphobia and homophobia are common with no legal protections.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's latest Nigeria travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex activity illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment; some northern states operate under Sharia law which can prescribe the death penalty; the SSMPA provides lengthy sentences extending to those who arrange, conduct or attend events perceived as same-sex weddings.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ Nigerians recount police abuses under 'weaponised' law
sources.claim_summary: TimesLIVE (March 2025): LGBTQ+ Nigerians recount police abuses under the 'weaponised' law - a 24-year-old man was stopped, beaten and forced to pay a bribe for 'looking gay'; the law creates a climate of hostility making LGBTQ+ people vulnerable to violations by police and the public.

sources.title: Job losses, rising attacks: 10 years of Nigeria's anti-LGBTQ law | Context by TRF
sources.claim_summary: Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024): 10 years of Nigeria's anti-LGBTQ law - the SSMPA has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, presenting LGBTQI persons as criminals; criminalisation blocks access to redress and justice; job prospects harmed; attacks increased since the law passed.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ Nigerians using apps like Grindr caught in dating traps | Context by TRF
sources.claim_summary: Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024): LGBTQ+ Nigerians battle dating-app traps ('kito') - violent entrapment via Grindr and other apps; victims are beaten, filmed, and blackmailed with threats to out them to family; community members fight back with exposure forums and sting operations.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.claim_summary: UK Home Office CPIN Nigeria: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics (June 2025, updated April 2026): official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Sept 2022) covers transgender Nigerians fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

sources.title: “Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe”: The Impact of Nigeria’s Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | HRW
sources.claim_summary: HRW report (Oct 2016) 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe': the impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act - the SSMPA's scope is far wider than marriage: it bans cohabitation, 'public show of same sex amorous relationship', and gay organisations (10-14 years); police torture and arbitrary arrests; vigilante groups added homosexuality to their 'terms of reference'.
